item.title: Journey to Antarctica! — Tue Sep 8, 6:00 PM — Innovation Lab
item.description:
Penguins! Parkas! Phenomenal science! Join us in the Innovation Lab (3rd floor) at Main Library for a presentation and discussion with Margaret Milikin, a logistics expert who works at McMurdo Station in Antarctica. Learn about Antarctica's wildlife, life at McMurdo, and what type of career path could lead YOU to this icy paradise.
Registration is required. We recommend this program for tweens (ages 9-12), teens, and adults.
This event will open to waitlisted registrants at 6:15pm, at which time seating will be first come, first served.
Please note, parking may be limited due to other library programming. If needed, you may park in the Queen Street Parking Deck (115 N. Queen St.) and the Library will validate your ticket.
If you have any accessibility questions or accommodation needs, please contact Jennifer at Accessibility_Services@dconc.gov. We ask that, if possible, all accommodation requests be made at least three (3) business days prior to the event.
Source: Libcal Durham

item.title: Songs We Carry: Exploring Music, Memory, and Family Stories — Tue Sep 8, 6:00 PM — Main Children's Programming Room
item.description:
What songs carry memories of the people and places that have shaped us? In this interactive workshop, participants will reflect on songs connected to family, home, heritage, or tradition and create a small collage-style memento that brings together music, memory, images, and words. Together, we’ll explore the ways songs can hold stories, connect generations, and become part of the everyday archives we carry with us.
Led by Duke music professor Dr. Sophia Enriquez, part of “Forum @ the Library” - a monthly series featuring Duke faculty sharing their work in an interactive format, hosted by the Library in partnership with Duke’s Forum for Scholars and Publics at the Franklin Humanities Institute.
Source: Libcal Durhamcountylibrary 14288

item.description:

item.description:
We invite you to view rare 19th-century prints of the Declaration of Independence at Durham County Main Library.
As part of We the People: A Duke & Durham Initiative, Durham County Main Library and the Nasher Museum of Art at Duke University are presenting three historic copies of the Declaration of Independence on loan from the David M. Rubenstein Americana Collection. This exhibition offers a rare opportunity to explore how the nation's founding document was visually rendered and circulated in early American history.
The exhibition will feature three rare prints on loan from the David M. Rubenstein Americana Collection: a rare official full-sized 1823 facsimile engraved by William J. Stone (known as a Stone Declaration) alongside two historic broadside copies from the same era: an 1818 reproduction by calligrapher Benjamin Owen Tyler and a more ornate 1819 illustrated version published by John Binns.

item.description:

item.title: Energy and Development in India: From National Policy to Local Impact — Thu Sep 10, 11:30 AM — Energy Hub Teaching Lab
item.description:
Duke community, join us for an engaging session with Divyanshu Jha, a senior Indian Administrative Service officer with the Government of India. Jha brings a unique perspective on energy and development, shaped by his experience at both the Indian Federal Ministry of New and Renewable Energy and at the local district administration level.
In this talk, Jha will examine how India can translate national policy and ambitious energy transition targets into meaningful change on the ground. He will discuss the opportunities and challenges involved in expanding clean energy, strengthening energy access, enabling sustainable economic growth, and implementing policy effectively at the local level.
The conversation will offer participants an opportunity to understand the energy transition through both a policy and implementation lens by connecting renewable energy ambitions with the everyday realities of governance, infrastructure, livelihoods, and development. item.description:
The NAMI Durham and NAMI On Campus youth leaders proudly present the You Are Not Alone Youth Mental Health Festival, a free community event created by youth, for youth, and the community. item.title: Downtown Durham African American Historian-Guided Tour — Sat Sep 12, 4:00 PM — CCB Plaza
item.description:
Durham: the mecca of black capitalism and the center of North Carolina’s African American business community. Join a local historian on this guided walking tour of Durham’s Black Wall Street, hearing the stories of how a humble sharecropper became the owner of the largest black-ned company in American history, and seeing some of the sites related to their stories. Learn how businessmen, labor organizers, educated academics, and craftsmen each contributed to the unique history of Durham’s African American community.
Source: Downtown Durham Inc

item.title: Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star (Theatre for the Very Young) — Sun Sep 13, 10:00 AM — Raleigh Little Theatre
item.description:
Twinkle, Twinkle, Little Star is an interactive children’s theatre piece for very young audiences, performed by two Star Keepers named Glimmer and Sparkle. It’s time for the night sky to fill with stars, but one important star — Little Star, the wishing star — is missing because Sparkle rushed through putting the stars away the previous morning and muddled everything up. What follows is a search-and-rescue adventure as the two star keepers (and the audience) hunt for Little Star, discovering along the way that all the other stars have been put in the wrong places too and need to be moved to their proper place. Audience members help the Star Keepers find and re-organize the sky just in time for nightfall so that everyone can make a wish on their favorite star. Twinkle, Twinkle explores the ideas that mistakes happen, feelings are valid, and no one has to face hard things alone – all wrapped up in a genuinely joyful romp about stars.
By Ernie Nolan Produced by special arrangemen

item.title: iNaturalist Together After Dark — Fri Sep 25, 7:00 PM — Prairie Ridge
item.description:
All programs at Prairie Ridge currently require registration. Register Join fellow iNaturalist users for an evening at Prairie Ridge as we investigate the wildlife that is active at night. We’ll sweep net for insects, take a short walk to the pond to listen for frogs and birds, and have light stations to attract moths and other nocturnal insects. Bring a flashlight and a smartphone or camera so you can photograph and document what you see. This program includes a brief introduction to iNaturalist, including a few advanced features you may not know about before we head out to the frog and insect stations. Show up with iNaturalist already installed on your phone and a flashlight for the best experience!
Source: NC Museum of Natural Sciences

item.description:
‘TWAS THE NIGHT BEFORE… is Cirque du Soleil’s first holiday show, based on the classic poem “A Visit from Saint Nicholas” by Clement Clarke Moore. Memorable lines from this cherished classic inspired Cirque’s story about a jaded young girl who rediscovers the magic of the holidays.
A festive flurry of love and cheer created especially for families, ‘TWAS THE NIGHT BEFORE… features thrilling acrobatics, lovable characters - and a soundtrack including holiday classics re-invented by Cirque du Soleil. The show was conceived and is directed by Cirque du Soleil Senior Artistic Director James Hadley, a 25-year veteran of circus productions and live theater.
This show will be in town for 17 performances across nine days. Note that showtimes vary. Get your tickets here!

item.title: Tuesday Computer Class @ Main — Tue Sep 8, 10:00 AM — Computer Lab
item.description:
Come join a supportive group environment for self-paced digital skills courses. We'll be using Northstar Digital Literacy, a free online resource available to all Durham County Library patrons. item.description:
Incubated at Duke, Pressing Prompts (pressingprompts.org) is an open education resource for instructors across all disciplines who are seeking ways to integrate AI ethics into their classrooms. Unlike a static set of "best practices," Pressing Prompts is grounded in principles of critical pedagogy and educational experimentation, encouraging instructors and students to examine how AI raises crucial questions about our academic responsibilities, knowledge, labor, judgment, and learning.
In this workshop, we will offer: a brief overview of Pressing Prompts within the larger context of AI, ethics, and education; scaffolded opportunities to experiment with Pressing Prompts to consider how it might fit into one of your classroom conversations, assignments, or larger course units; and a facilitated conversation for sharing ideas between faculty peers.

What follows is a search-and-rescue adventure as the two star keepers (and the audience) hunt for Little Star, discovering along the way that all the other stars have been put in the wrong places too and need to be moved to their proper place. Audience members help the Star Keepers find and re-organize the sky just in time for nightfall so that everyone can make a wish on their favorite star. Twinkle, Twinkle explores the ideas that mistakes happen, feelings are valid, and no one has to face hard things alone – all wrapped up in a genuinely joyful romp about stars.

item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Sat Dec 5 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.
